explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Paul says, "be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power." (Ephesians 6:10) Notice where the strength comes from. It isn't from flexing in the mirror or from a pep talk to yourself. It comes from the Lord, and that's a relief to me, because my arms are made of mustache.

Samson was an Israelite judge, and his strength was tied to his hair never being cut (Judges 16:17). Paul doesn't point the believers to a strongman at all. He says to be strong "in the Lord and in His mighty power." (Ephesians 6:10) Even the strongest man in the Bible didn't make the list here, friend.

Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon (Daniel 1:1), and he had an army and a throne. Paul doesn't send the believers to any king's power, though. He says to be strong "in the Lord and in His mighty power." (Ephesians 6:10) That's the only power on this card worth leaning on, baker.

explanations.answer: To stand against the devil's schemes
explanations.explanation: That's the one! Paul says to put on the full armor of God "so that you can make your stand against the devil's schemes." (Ephesians 6:11) The armor has a job, and the job is standing. Schemes are plans, so I think Paul wants the believers ready for whatever the devil cooks up.

explanations.answer: To win the respect of the city
explanations.explanation: Paul never brings up the city's opinion here. He gives the reason himself: "so that you can make your stand against the devil's schemes." (Ephesians 6:11) This armor isn't for looking impressive on the street, friend. It's for standing.

Close, but Paul isn't talking about leaders here. He says "you" can make your stand, and he's writing to the believers. The reason he gives is "against the devil's schemes." (Ephesians 6:11) Every believer reading that letter gets a set of armor, baker.

Almost, but Paul says the opposite. He writes, "our struggle is not against flesh and blood." (Ephesians 6:12) The word "not" is doing the heavy lifting in that sentence. So the believers aren't fighting the people they can see.

That's right! Paul says, "For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world's darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms." (Ephesians 6:12) That's a long list, and not one of them is a neighbor. Good catch, baker.

Yes, baker! Paul says the struggle is against the rulers, the authorities, the powers of this world's darkness, "and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms." (Ephesians 6:12) He says it plainly. This fight happens where you can't see it, so the armor is spiritual too.

Hard times are real, friend, and I won't pretend otherwise. But Paul doesn't list them here. He names rulers, authorities, the powers of this world's darkness, and "the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms." (Ephesians 6:12)

That one tempts plenty of folks, but Paul doesn't name it in this passage. What he names is "the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms," along with the rulers, authorities and powers of this world's darkness. (Ephesians 6:12) So the struggle he describes here is bigger than anything in our wallets, baker.

That's it! Paul says to take up the armor "so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground." (Ephesians 6:13) He says "when," not "if." So the armor gets put on ahead of time, baker, just like an oven gets preheated.

A day of rest sounds lovely, friend, but that isn't what Paul wrote. He says, "so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground." (Ephesians 6:13) You don't need a full set of armor to take a nap. The day Paul has in mind is the day of evil.

A harvest is a happy day, baker, and I'd gladly stand around for one. But Paul says, "when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground." (Ephesians 6:13) That's why the armor is part of the picture.

Yes! Paul says, "with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace." (Ephesians 6:15) Peace goes on the feet, and I'm told that's good news for every other piece of armor above them. So the believers aren't just standing there. They're ready.

Moses was Israel's leader, but Paul doesn't bring him up in this passage. The thing fitted on the feet is "the readiness of the gospel of peace." (Ephesians 6:15) Peace is right there in the name, baker.
Paul isn't talking about a kingdom here. He says the feet are fitted "with the readiness of the gospel of peace." (Ephesians 6:15) Think of it as shoes for the good news, friend.

That's right, baker! Paul says, "take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one." (Ephesians 6:16) All of them, friend, not just the small ones. I'd want that shield in my hand.
It's actually true. Paul says the shield of faith is how "you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one." (Ephesians 6:16) Notice that he says "all." He doesn't say some or most, baker.

Yes! Paul says the sword of the Spirit "is the word of God." (Ephesians 6:17) Baker, that's why you're here, picking up the Word one passage at a time. It's the only piece of armor on the list that Paul says to take up and swing.
Glory sounds like a good fit for a sword, I'll give you that. But Paul says the sword of the Spirit "is the word of God." (Ephesians 6:17) He doesn't mention glory at all, friend.
Wisdom is a fine thing to carry, baker, but it's not what Paul wrote. He says the sword of the Spirit "is the word of God." (Ephesians 6:17) So the sword is the Word itself.

Not quite, baker. Paul says, "Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition." (Ephesians 6:18) At all times covers the quiet days too. The day of evil isn't the only time he has in mind.

That's right! Paul says to "Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition." (Ephesians 6:18) At all times means all times, friend, not just the rough ones. I think that makes prayer more like a daily habit than an emergency button.

You got it, baker! Paul says to "stay alert with all perseverance in your prayers for all the saints." (Ephesians 6:18) That means they're praying for each other too. The prayer list is as wide as the whole family of believers.
Paul doesn't point them to the elders of Israel. He says to stay alert and keep at it "in your prayers for all the saints." (Ephesians 6:18) All of them, friend, with nobody left off the list.
Paul doesn't mention kings anywhere in this passage, baker. He says the prayers are "for all the saints." (Ephesians 6:18) That's the whole crowd of believers.

explanations.answer: Words to share the gospel boldly
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker! Paul asks them to pray "that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel." (Ephesians 6:19) Think about that. Paul asks for help with the words, and that's what he puts first.

explanations.answer: A safe way out of his trouble
explanations.explanation: Paul does call himself "an ambassador in chains" (Ephesians 6:20), so he's in a tough spot. But his request is about words, not an escape. He asks that "words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel." (Ephesians 6:19)

Paul doesn't say anything about travel in this part. What he asks for is "words…given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel." (Ephesians 6:19) It's about boldness and the right words, friend.

Yes, baker! Paul says the gospel is the thing "for which I am an ambassador in chains." (Ephesians 6:20) An ambassador speaks for the one who sent him. So even in chains, Paul still has a message to deliver.
Shepherd is a lovely title, friend, but Paul doesn't use it for himself here. He says, "for which I am an ambassador in chains." (Ephesians 6:20) Chains are the part that makes this one stand out.
A watchman is a real job in the Bible, baker, but Paul doesn't claim it here. He says the gospel is what he's "an ambassador in chains" for. (Ephesians 6:20) That's the title on this card.

explanations.answer: To tell them about Paul and encourage them
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker! Paul says, "I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts." (Ephesians 6:22) Tychicus brings the news and the encouragement together. A good friend delivers both.

explanations.answer: To collect a gift for Paul's trial
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention a gift or a trial in this part of the letter. He says Tychicus will "tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing." (Ephesians 6:21) He adds that Tychicus "may encourage your hearts." (Ephesians 6:22)

explanations.answer: To choose new leaders for their church
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give Tychicus that job. The reason he states is "that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts." (Ephesians 6:22) He's coming to share news and cheer them up, friend.

explanations.answer: God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Paul writes, "Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." (Ephesians 6:23) That's where it comes from. It's not something the believers have to bake up on their own.

explanations.answer: Peter and the church in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, is never mentioned in this passage. Paul says the peace and love with faith come "from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." (Ephesians 6:23) That's the source, friend.
Moses, Israel's leader, doesn't show up in Paul's closing. He says the peace and love with faith come "from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." (Ephesians 6:23) Straight from the top, baker.

Not quite, friend. Paul's last words are "Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love." (Ephesians 6:24) He says all who love Him, not just the leaders. That means the door is wide open.

That's right, baker! Paul ends with "Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love." (Ephesians 6:24) He says "all," so nobody gets left out of the last line. That's a good way to end a letter.
